conventions.convention: Increasing and decreasing mean strictly increasing and strictly decreasing; monotone permits either weak direction.

Continuity is relative to the domain and uses unpunctured neighbourhoods. Classification uses only sides on which the point is a limit point; endpoint discontinuities of the first kind are not called jumps.
Oscillation uses extended-real suprema and infima, includes the centre in point neighbourhoods, and assigns oscillation −∞ to the empty set.
Thomae's denominator is the least positive natural q for which qx is an integer, equivalently the positive denominator in lowest terms.
The Darboux property requires the image of every order-convex subinterval to be order-convex.
Upper semicontinuity bounds nearby values strictly above by f(c)+ε; lower semicontinuity bounds them strictly below by f(c)−ε, relative to the domain.
Sequences of functions start at index 0; pointwise convergence allows the eventual index to depend on the point.
Hamel basis existence assumes AC. Coordinates use injective finite lists, and a fixed basis vector has a uniquely determined rational coefficient map.
Prescribed jump masses are 2^(−k−1), indexed from 0, and collected when s(k)<x. The resulting function is left continuous, including at its jumps.

load_bearing.statement: For nondecreasing f on an order-convex I and c∈I, each nonempty side makes its one-sided limit well posed: the left limit is the supremum of values below c and is ≤f(c); the right limit is the infimum of values above c and is ≥f(c).
Let A⊆ℝ, f:A→ℝ and c∈A. Then f is continuous at c if and only if ω_f(c)=0.
For f:A→ℝ and real ε>0, there is a closed G⊆ℝ with {x∈A:ω_f(x)≥ε}=A∩G.
The discontinuity set is the union of {x∈A:ω_f(x)≥1/(n+1)} over n∈ℕ. It is A∩F for an Fσ set F⊆ℝ, and the continuity set is A∩V for the complementary Gδ set V.
If f:ℝ→ℝ is additive and bounded above on [p,r] for reals p<r, then f(x)=f(1)x for every real x.

Assuming AC, ℝ has a basis B over its canonical rational subfield. For each b★∈B, every real has a unique decomposition λb★+w with λ∈ℚ and w∈span(B∖{b★}); its coefficient map is additive, rationally homogeneous, onto ℚ, and its kernel is nontrivial.
If a<b and a sequence of closed subsets F_n of ℝ covers [a,b], some F_n∩[a,b] contains a nondegenerate closed interval.
For every at most countable E⊆ℝ there is a nondecreasing f:ℝ→[0,1], continuous exactly outside E, with left limit f(c) strictly below its right limit at each c∈E.

For additive f:ℝ→ℝ, each of continuity at one point, monotonicity on a nondegenerate interval, an upper bound on one, a lower bound on one, constant sign on one, and a nondense graph implies f(x)=f(1)x everywhere.

For a<b and Baire class one f:[a,b]→ℝ, each positive oscillation superlevel set is closed and nowhere dense, the discontinuity set is meager, and the continuity set is dense in [a,b] and is the trace of a Gδ subset of ℝ.

concerns.concern: The paragraph 'On the phrase dense Gδ' says: 'It is not claimed that C is Gδ as a subset of ℝ, nor that it is dense in ℝ; neither is true in general, since C⊆[a,b].' The denial of absolute Gδ status is false. Claim 4 gives C=[a,b]∩V, and [a,b]=⋂_{n≥1}(a−1/n,b+1/n) is itself Gδ. Interleaving these open sets with those defining V proves that C is always Gδ in ℝ. The four numbered conclusions and their proof are unaffected.

The first Remark says 'a closed set may be nowhere dense in ℝ and yet fill an interval'. For a nondegenerate interval this is false: containing [u,v] with u<v forces nonempty interior. The same Remark subsequently acknowledges that containing a nondegenerate closed subinterval and having nonempty interior are equivalent here. The lemma's proof itself is sound.

The extension to nonincreasing functions says to take 'the two one-sided limits exchanged and all inequalities reversed'. These are two reversals where only one is appropriate. Literally applying both to L−≤f(c)≤L+ gives L+≥f(c)≥L−, which is false for a downward step. Keeping the side labels fixed and reversing inequalities gives the correct L−≥f(c)≥L+. The nondecreasing proof is sound.

The 'More precisely' paragraph, under the hypothesis that f is monotone in either direction, calls (lim-left f, lim-right f) 'a nonempty open interval' at every interior discontinuity. For the nonincreasing step f(x)=1 for x<0 and f(x)=0 for x≥0, that interval at 0 is (1,0), hence empty. Proof 1.1 correctly reduces to −f, but the additional assertion in the Statement does not carry that reduction.

The explanatory paragraph after the equivalence says 'the sets {x:ω_f(x)≥ε} are closed', although the item allows arbitrary A⊆ℝ. They are relatively closed, as the cited lemma explicitly states. For A=(0,1) and the restricted Dirichlet function, the superlevel set at ε=1 is (0,1), which is not closed in ℝ. Also L4 attributes the triangle inequality to lem-of-abs-value, whose Statement and proof do not establish it; the separate opened supplier is lem-of-triangle-inequality.

The first Remark says 'S_α is a subset of A, so it cannot be open in ℝ unless A is'. This is false. Take A=[0,1] and f≡0: for α=0, S_α=∅ is open although A is not. The intended statement that relative openness need not imply ambient openness is correct, as are the theorem and proof.

The first Remark says 'The proof uses nothing about f except that it is additive and not linear; every other property is read off thm-cauchy-functional-equation-regularity by contraposition.' This is false for claim 4. Rational range and dense level sets use the specific coefficient-map structure and nontrivial kernel in steps 2.2–2.3 and 3.3–4.1. Additive nonlinear maps can be injective: under the same AC assumption, swap two vectors of a Hamel basis and fix the others. The resulting rational-linear automorphism is nonlinear over ℝ and has singleton fibres.

The first Remark unconditionally says 'Measure zero is preserved by countable unions' and cites thm-countable-union-of-null-is-null. That published supplier explicitly begins 'Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice'. The example does not assume it. The cited general closure claim needs that qualification under the library's choice bookkeeping; the actual Cantor-image example does not use the closure claim.

The first Remark explains the separate graph argument by saying 'a non-dense graph gives no bound on f anywhere'. Literally this contradicts the proved implication: an additive function with nondense graph is linear, hence bounded on every bounded interval. The proof establishes density contrapositively without first deriving a bound; that distinction should replace the categorical wording.

alerts.finding: In cor-q-is-meager-and-not-g-delta, the second Remark says 'Uncountability and being residual are independent properties'. For subsets of ℝ this is false: every residual set is uncountable. If a residual set S were countable, S would be meager by its enumeration into nowhere dense singletons, while ℝ∖S is meager by residuality. Their union ℝ would then be meager, contradicting thm-baire-category-r. The displayed examples establish that an uncountable set need not be residual, but cannot establish independence in both directions.
